records.name: Olaudah Equiano (Gustavus Vassa)
records.scaleNote: Author of the best-known Middle Passage narrative (1789; nine British editions in his lifetime) and a leader of London's Black abolitionists; his African birth is debated by scholars.
records.origins: By his own account Equiano was born in an Igbo village in the hinterland of the Bight of Biafra (today south-eastern Nigeria), kidnapped with his sister at about eleven and passed through African owners to the coast. He was shipped to Barbados and then Virginia.
records.role_summary: Sold to Royal Navy lieutenant Michael Pascal, who renamed him Gustavus Vassa, he served at sea in the Seven Years' War, was sold to the Quaker merchant Robert King of Montserrat and bought his own freedom in 1766. In London he alerted Granville Sharp to the Zong killings (1783), was briefly commissary for the Sierra Leone resettlement (1786–87) and published 'The Interesting Narrative' (1789), touring Britain and Ireland to sell it and argue for abolition.

roleDetail.d: He bought his freedom from Robert King for £40, money earned through small trading on King's ships.
Its description of the slave-ship hold became one of the most quoted Middle Passage testimonies of the abolition campaign.

Vincent Carretta found a 1759 baptismal record and a 1773 naval muster giving his birthplace as (South) Carolina, and suggests the African chapters may draw on others' testimony; critics such as Paul Lovejoy argue the Igbo account is credible and the records unreliable. The question is unresolved.

records.legacy: Equiano married Susannah Cullen in 1792; their daughter Anna Maria died young, and Joanna Vassa survived to inherit his estate. He is commemorated by plaques in London and elsewhere, and his narrative is read in schools and universities in Britain, Nigeria and the United States.

legacyDetail.d: Westminster Abbey notes that his place of burial is not recorded.
His book is widely credited with helping build support for the 1807 Act, though it was one voice among many.

sources.label: Westminster Abbey — Olaudah Equiano (Gustavus Vassa)
UNC Documenting the American South — The Interesting Narrative (summary)
Wikipedia — Olaudah Equiano

records.name: Quobna Ottobah Cugoano
records.scaleNote: Author of 'Thoughts and Sentiments on the Evil and Wicked Traffic of the Slavery' (1787), the most radical abolitionist book of its era by an African author; little is known of his later life.
records.origins: Born in the Fante town of Ajumako (present-day Ghana), Cugoano was kidnapped at about thirteen in 1770 and taken to Cape Coast, where he was sold to Europeans and shipped to Grenada.
records.role_summary: After about a year on Grenada plantations he was taken to England in 1772 by Alexander Campbell, baptised John Stuart in 1773 and became free, working as a servant to the painters Richard and Maria Cosway. With Equiano he was a founder of the Sons of Africa and in 1787 published a book demanding immediate abolition and emancipation and arguing that the enslaved had a right to resist.

roleDetail.d: His book describes his kidnapping, the Cape Coast fort, and the screams of captives as the ship sailed.
Unlike most British campaigners of 1787, who targeted only the trade, he called for the end of slavery itself.
He and Granville Sharp helped stop the forced shipment of a Black man from London to the Caribbean.

records.legacy: Cugoano disappears from the record after 1791; his date and place of death are unknown. His book is now a core text in histories of Black political thought and is studied in philosophy as well as history.

legacyDetail.d: The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy now carries an entry on him as a political philosopher.

sources.label: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy — Ottobah Cugoano
London Museum — Ottobah Cugoano: a powerful critic of slavery

records.name: Ayuba Suleiman Diallo (Job ben Solomon)
records.scaleNote: Subject of Thomas Bluett's 'Some Memoirs of the Life of Job' (1734) and of William Hoare's 1733 portrait, the earliest known British oil portrait of a freed enslaved African Muslim.
records.origins: Son of a Muslim cleric of Bundu in the Senegal–Gambia hinterland, Ayuba was a literate Fula trader who had himself travelled to the Gambia in 1730/31 to sell two enslaved people to an English captain.
records.role_summary: On the way home he was seized by Mandinka raiders and sold to the same English ship, which carried him to Annapolis, Maryland, where he worked on a tobacco farm. After an escape attempt he was jailed in Kent County, where Thomas Bluett noted his Arabic writing; a letter he wrote to his father reached James Oglethorpe of the Royal African Company, who arranged his purchase. In London he was received by scholars and the royal family before returning to Gambia on a Company ship in 1734.

roleDetail.d: His story shows how African merchants could themselves be swept into the trade they took part in.

roleDetail.t: Freed through the Royal African Company.
roleDetail.d: Oglethorpe bought him; a London subscription repaid his purchase and costs, and he went home as a Company associate.
Hoare's portrait shows him with a Qur'an he wrote out from memory; it is on long-term loan from Qatar Museums to the National Portrait Gallery.

records.legacy: Ayuba lived until c. 1773 in Bundu, corresponding with British contacts. His portrait was bought by Qatar Museums in 2009, placed under a UK export bar and lent to the National Portrait Gallery, where it has been shown and toured since 2011.

legacyDetail.t: Earliest British portrait of a freed African.
legacyDetail.d: Displayed and toured by the National Portrait Gallery as a key image of Black British history.

sources.label: UNC Documenting the American South — Thomas Bluett, Some Memoirs of the Life of Job (1734)
SlaveVoyages — Ayuba Suleiman Diallo and Slavery in the Atlantic World
National Portrait Gallery — Ayuba Suleiman Diallo

records.name: Abd al-Rahman Ibrahima Ibn Sori
records.scaleNote: Enslaved for c. 40 years in Mississippi; his release became a national cause in 1828 and is documented in newspapers, letters and the 2007 PBS film 'Prince Among Slaves'.
records.origins: A son of the almaami (ruler) of the Islamic state of Futa Jallon in present-day Guinea, he studied in Timbuktu and became a cavalry commander.
records.role_summary: Captured in an ambush in 1788, he was sold to British traders, shipped across the Atlantic and eventually sold to Thomas Foster near Natchez, where he worked for some forty years, becoming the plantation's overseer and marrying an enslaved woman, Isabella. Newspaper editor Andrew Marschalk forwarded an Arabic letter he wrote; interest from the Sultan of Morocco led President John Quincy Adams's administration to arrange his release in 1828.

roleDetail.d: His royal birth was known in Natchez but brought no freedom for decades.
Freed with Isabella, he toured northern cities to raise money to buy his children, but most remained enslaved.

records.legacy: He sailed for Liberia with the American Colonization Society and died in Monrovia in 1829 before reaching Futa Jallon. Some descendants were later freed and joined him in Liberia; others remained in Mississippi. Natchez unveiled a historical marker to him in 2025.

legacyDetail.d: Terry Alford's 1977 biography and a 2007 PBS film brought his story to wide audiences.

sources.label: Mississippi History Now — A Prince Enslaved in Southwest Mississippi
Mississippi Today — Natchez honors 'prince among slaves' (2025)
Wikipedia — Abdulrahman Ibrahim Ibn Sori

records.name: Omar ibn Said
records.scaleNote: Wrote 'The Life of Omar ibn Said' (1831), the only known autobiography written in Arabic by a person enslaved in the US; the Library of Congress acquired his papers in 2017.
records.origins: Born to a wealthy Muslim family in Futa Toro on the Senegal River, Omar studied for some 25 years and worked as a scholar and teacher.
records.role_summary: Captured in war in 1807 at about 37, he was shipped to Charleston, South Carolina, in the last months before the US import ban. He escaped a cruel enslaver in 1810 and walked to Fayetteville, North Carolina, where he was jailed; James Owen of Bladen County then bought him. He lived the rest of his life enslaved by the Owen family, who presented him as a Christian convert, while he continued writing in Arabic, including Qur'anic passages.

roleDetail.d: The Arabic he wrote on the walls of the Fayetteville jail drew local attention to him.
His 15-page text opens with a Qur'anic sura (al-Mulk) on God's sovereignty, read by scholars as a quiet comment on his enslavement.

records.legacy: His papers (42 documents) are digitised by the Library of Congress. A Fayetteville mosque was renamed Masjid Omar ibn Sayyid, a North Carolina highway marker commemorates him, and an opera, 'Omar' by Rhiannon Giddens and Michael Abels, won the 2023 Pulitzer Prize for Music.

legacyDetail.d: The Omar ibn Said Collection was put online in 2019.
'Omar' premiered at Spoleto Festival USA in Charleston in 2022.

sources.label: NCpedia — Said, Omar Ibn
Library of Congress — The Life of Omar Ibn Said (manuscript record)
UNC Documenting the American South — Omar ibn Said collection

records.name: Venture Smith (Broteer Furro)
records.scaleNote: His 1798 'Narrative', dictated to Elisha Niles, is among the earliest African-American slave narratives; his grave and land records survive in Connecticut.
records.origins: Born Broteer, son of a ruler in 'Dukandarra' in the West African interior (location uncertain), he was captured as a child of about eight when raiders attacked his father's town.
records.role_summary: Marched to the coast and sold at Anomabu on the Gold Coast to Robertson Mumford, steward of a Rhode Island ship, for four gallons of rum and a piece of calico, he was named 'Venture' as Mumford's private venture. Taken via Barbados to Rhode Island and Fishers Island, he was sold several times before Oliver Smith of Stonington let him buy his freedom in 1765; he then bought his wife Meg and their children.

roleDetail.d: He paid for himself, his wife and children and others, then acquired more than 100 acres in East Haddam.
His narrative and later research link him to a Newport-area voyage (often identified as the Charming Susanna).

records.legacy: He died in 1805 and is buried at First Church cemetery, East Haddam, under a stone calling him 'son of a king'. Descendants hold an annual Venture Smith Day and family reunions; a 2006 exhumation for DNA study did not yield usable results.

legacyDetail.d: Connecticut Public reported on descendants' work to teach his narrative (2024).

sources.label: UNC Documenting the American South — A Narrative of the Life and Adventures of Venture
ConnecticutHistory.org — Venture Smith: from slavery to freedom
Connecticut Public — Descendants keep Venture Smith's story alive (2024)

connections.label: carried on a Rhode Island ship

records.name: Phillis Wheatley
records.scaleNote: First African American (and among the first American women) to publish a book of poetry, 'Poems on Various Subjects, Religious and Moral' (London, 1773); her ship and purchase are documented.
records.origins: Born around 1753 in West Africa, most likely in present-day Senegal or Gambia, she was taken at about seven or eight.
records.role_summary: She arrived in Boston on 11 July 1761 aboard the slave ship Phillis, owned by Timothy Fitch and captained by Peter Gwinn, and was bought by the merchant John Wheatley for his wife Susanna, who named her after the ship. Taught to read English, Latin and the Bible, she published her first poem in 1767 and travelled to London in 1773 where her book appeared; she was freed shortly afterwards and in 1776 met George Washington.

roleDetail.d: Her first name came from the vessel that carried her across the Atlantic.
Her book carried an attestation by 18 Boston men that she had written the poems; Jefferson later dismissed her work.

records.legacy: She married John Peters, struggled to publish a second volume and died in poverty in Boston in 1784. She is honoured in the Boston Women's Memorial (2003), a London blue plaque (2019) and a US postage stamp (2026), and is now read as a founding figure of African-American literature.

legacyDetail.d: Boston Women's Memorial sculpture, schools and YWCAs bear her name.

sources.label: Poets.org — Phillis Wheatley
Society of Early Americanists — Wheatley Chronology
Wikipedia — Phillis Wheatley

records.name: Mahommah Gardo Baquaqua
records.scaleNote: His 'Biography' (Detroit, 1854), edited by Samuel Moore, is the only known first-person narrative of a person enslaved in Brazil published in English; re-edited by Robin Law and Paul Lovejoy (2001/2007).
records.origins: Born to a Muslim trading family in Zoogoo (Djougou), in present-day northern Benin, he served as a bodyguard to a local ruler before being captured in the mid-1840s.
records.role_summary: Taken south to Ouidah and shipped to Pernambuco, Brazil, he was sold to a baker who abused him, then to a ship captain in Rio de Janeiro. In 1847 his ship sailed to New York, where Black and white abolitionists went to court for him and the crew; he escaped to Haiti, converted to Christianity with Baptist missionaries, studied at New York Central College and dictated his life story.

roleDetail.d: His description of the hold on the voyage from Ouidah to Brazil is a rare first-person account of the illegal South Atlantic trade.
Abolitionists' legal action after his ship docked in 1847 enabled his escape.

records.legacy: He was last recorded in Britain in 1857, still hoping to return to Africa; his fate is unknown. His narrative is studied in Brazil, Benin and North America and has been republished in Portuguese.

legacyDetail.d: Law and Lovejoy traced his life through Djougou, Brazil and New York archives.

sources.label: UNC Documenting the American South — Biography of Mahommah G. Baquaqua (summary)
Project MUSE — The Biography of Mahommah Gardo Baquaqua

records.name: Sengbe Pieh (Joseph Cinqué)
records.scaleNote: Leader of the 1839 Amistad revolt; the case (United States v. The Amistad, 1841) is one of the most documented slave-trade cases, with court records at the US National Archives.
records.origins: A Mende rice farmer, married with three children, he was seized in 1839 (by his account for a debt) and sold through the Vai ruler King Siaka to the Spanish trader Pedro Blanco at the Gallinas.
records.role_summary: He was shipped illegally on the Portuguese slaver Tecora to Havana, where José Ruiz and Pedro Montes bought him and 52 others under false papers and put them aboard the schooner Amistad. In July 1839 he led the uprising that killed Captain Ramón Ferrer and the cook; the ship was seized off Long Island, and after two years of litigation the US Supreme Court ruled in March 1841 that the Africans had been illegally enslaved and were free.

roleDetail.d: Spain had banned slave imports to Cuba from 1820; the 'ladino' papers falsely called the captives long-resident Cubans.
Adams and Roger Sherman Baldwin argued the case before the Supreme Court.
Thirty-five survivors sailed home with missionaries in late 1841, reaching Freetown in January 1842.

records.legacy: Back in Sierra Leone he found his family gone amid war; little is certain about his later life and claims that he became a slave trader are considered implausible by historians. He has appeared on Sierra Leone's banknotes, has statues in New Haven and Hartford, and the replica schooner Amistad sails from Connecticut as an education ship.

legacyDetail.d: His portrait on currency marks his status as a symbol of resistance.

sources.label: US National Archives — Teaching With Documents: The Amistad Case
National Park Service — Amistad: How it Began (source list and travel itinerary)
Wikipedia — Sengbe Pieh

records.name: Oluale Kossola (Cudjo Lewis)
records.scaleNote: Interviewed by Zora Neale Hurston (1927–28) for 'Barracoon' (written 1931, published 2018); her 1928 film of him is among the very few moving images of a Middle Passage survivor (Redoshi was filmed in 1938).
records.origins: Kossola was Yoruba of the Isha sub-group from the Banté region of present-day Benin. In 1860 a Dahomean army attacked his town, killing many, and marched survivors to Ouidah.
records.role_summary: Held about three weeks in a barracoon at Ouidah, he was sold to William Foster and carried on the Clotilda to Mobile in July 1860, decades after the US ban. Enslaved by James Meaher until Union troops arrived in 1865, he and fellow survivors asked Timothy Meaher for land as reparation and were refused; they bought land and founded African Town.

roleDetail.d: His request to Meaher for land is one of the earliest recorded reparations demands by survivors of the trade.
Injured by a train, he sued the railroad company for damages.

records.legacy: He died in 1935 and is buried in Africatown's Old Plateau Cemetery. Descendants still live in Mobile, the Africatown Heritage House (opened 2023) features his story, and Hurston's 'Barracoon' became a bestseller.

legacyDetail.d: Hurston's book, unpublished for 87 years, gives his account in his own dialect.

sources.label: Encyclopedia of Alabama — Cudjo Lewis
Smithsonian Magazine — Zora Neale Hurston's 'Barracoon'

records.name: Redoshi (Sally Smith)
records.nation: Bight of Benin (West Africa, exact people uncertain)
records.scaleNote: Identified in 2019 by Hannah Durkin from census records, a memoir by Amelia Boynton Robinson and a 1938 USDA film; long thought the last Clotilda survivor.
records.origins: Kidnapped at about twelve in a raid on her village in West Africa in 1860, she was taken to Ouidah.
records.role_summary: Shipped on the Clotilda, she was bought by Washington M. Smith, a Selma banker who owned a plantation at Bogue Chitto, and forced into marriage with an older African man. After emancipation she remained on the land with her husband and daughter, farming and keeping her African identity.

roleDetail.d: She appears in the USDA film 'The Negro Farmer' — the only known footage of a female Middle Passage survivor.
Durkin's 2019 article in Slavery & Abolition named her and traced her life.

records.legacy: She died in 1937. Her story is part of the wider Clotilda descendant movement around Africatown and Selma, and of the 2022 film 'Descendant'.

legacyDetail.d: Durkin later identified Matilda McCrear as outliving her by three years.

sources.label: Smithsonian Magazine — Researcher identifies last American woman to survive the African slave trade
History.com — The last slave ship survivor: Redoshi

records.name: Matilda McCrear (Àbáké)
records.scaleNote: Identified by Hannah Durkin (2020) as the last known survivor of the transatlantic slave trade, mainly from a 1931 Selma Times-Journal interview and census data.
records.origins: Born Àbáké around 1857, a Yoruba child, she was taken at about two with her mother Gracie and sisters.
records.role_summary: Carried on the Clotilda, she, her mother and one sister were bought by Memorable Walker Creagh and enslaved near Selma; two other sisters were sold away and never seen again. After emancipation she took the name McCrear, kept Yoruba hair-wrapping traditions, had a long partnership with a German-born man, Jacob Schuler, and raised many children.

roleDetail.d: In her 70s she walked to Selma's courthouse to seek compensation as a Clotilda survivor; the claim was dismissed.

records.legacy: She died in January 1940 in poverty. Her grandson Johnny Crear learned of her Clotilda origins only from Durkin's research; the Equal Justice Initiative and others now commemorate her.

legacyDetail.d: Her death in 1940 is the latest documented for anyone carried in the transatlantic trade.

sources.label: Equal Justice Initiative — Remembering the last survivor of the transatlantic slave trade
Archaeology Magazine — Survivor of transatlantic trade identified (2020)
Wikipedia — Matilda McCrear

records.name: Belinda Sutton
records.nation: Gold Coast / Volta region (probably Ewe or Akan)
records.scaleNote: Her 1783 petition to the Massachusetts General Court is one of the earliest successful claims for reparations by a formerly enslaved person in North America.
records.origins: Her petition says she was kidnapped at about twelve from a village near the Volta River (in present-day Ghana or Togo) and survived the crossing.
records.role_summary: She was enslaved by the Royall family, first in Antigua and then at their Medford estate, for some fifty years. Isaac Royall Jr fled as a Loyalist in 1775; in February 1783 she dictated a petition asking for an allowance from his confiscated estate 'which has been augmented by her servitude', signing with her mark.

roleDetail.d: The legislature awarded her an annual pension (c. £15), but payments lapsed and she had to petition repeatedly over a decade.
Research found her married name, Sutton, now used in preference to her enslaver's surname.

records.legacy: Her petition is widely reprinted as an early reparations text, and the Royall House and Slave Quarters museum in Medford interprets her life.

legacyDetail.d: Historians cite her award in modern reparations debates.

sources.label: Royall House and Slave Quarters — Belinda Sutton and her petitions
Medford Historical Society — The mark of Belinda Sutton

records.name: John Newton
records.scaleNote: Mate and then master on four Liverpool slaving voyages 1748–54 (Brownlow, Duke of Argyle, African), per his journals and SlaveVoyages; later a leading clerical voice for abolition.
records.origins: A sailor's son from Wapping, Newton was pressed into the Royal Navy, then worked for a slave trader on the Plantain Islands off Sierra Leone, where he was himself mistreated. A storm in 1748 began his evangelical conversion, but he stayed in the trade.
records.role_summary: He commanded the Duke of Argyle (1750) and the African (1752–54) for Liverpool merchant Joseph Manesty, buying captives along the Windward and Sierra Leone coasts and suppressing attempted revolts with chains and thumbscrews, as his own journal records. Ill health ended his sea career in 1754.

roleDetail.d: His logs of 1750–54 are a key source on buying and holding captives on the Sierra Leone coast.
In 'Thoughts upon the African Slave Trade' (1788) he confessed his role and testified to Parliament; he had not opposed the trade while in it.

records.legacy: Ordained in 1764, he wrote 'Amazing Grace' for the Olney Hymns (1779) and mentored William Wilberforce. He died in 1807, the year the British trade was abolished; the hymn's popularity has often obscured his slaving years.

legacyDetail.d: The hymn is frequently, but inaccurately, presented as written in response to the slave trade.

sources.label: Royal Museums Greenwich — Thoughts upon the African Slave Trade
Rochester Cathedral — John Newton (1725–1807)
Wikipedia — John Newton
Royal Museums Greenwich — John Newton's journal, Duke of Argyle and African, 1750–1754 (LOG/M/46)

lineage.name: John Newton the Elder
lineage.note: A shipmaster in the Mediterranean service who took his son to sea at eleven and retired in 1742; it was through his friendship with Joseph Manesty that the younger Newton entered the slave trade.

lineage.name: Amos Clow (Clowe)
lineage.note: A slave trader on the Plantain Islands off Sierra Leone who took Newton on in 1745 and left him with his African wife, known as Princess Peye of the Sherbro, under whom Newton was himself held in servitude.

lineage.name: Joseph Manesty
lineage.note: Liverpool merchant and friend of Newton's father who got him the mate's berth on the Brownlow (1748), gave him command of the Duke of Argyle and the African (1750–54), and in 1755 helped him become tide surveyor at Liverpool; Newton kept investing in Manesty's slaving voyages after leaving the sea.

lineage.name: Mary Catlett
lineage.note: His childhood sweetheart, married in February 1750 just before his first command; he wrote her letters throughout his slaving voyages, and they were buried together.

lineage.name: John Thornton
lineage.note: Evangelical merchant who supplemented Newton's stipend at Olney and in 1779 presented him to the rectory of St Mary Woolnoth in the City of London, which he held until his death.

lineage.name: William Cowper
lineage.note: The poet moved to Olney in 1767 to be near Newton; together they published the Olney Hymns (1779), which include 'Amazing Grace'.

lineage.name: Elizabeth Cunningham and Eliza Catlett
lineage.note: Two orphaned nieces from his wife's family whom the childless Newtons adopted and raised in London.

lineage.name: William Wilberforce
lineage.note: Newton counselled the young MP after his conversion to stay in Parliament, and his 1788 pamphlet 'Thoughts upon the African Slave Trade', sent to every MP, fed the abolition campaign Wilberforce led.

records.today: Newton had no children of his own, and no publicly documented descendants have been traced. He and Mary were first buried at St Mary Woolnoth and reinterred at Olney's parish church of St Peter and St Paul in 1893; his journal of the Duke of Argyle and African voyages is held by the National Maritime Museum, Greenwich. His fame now rests on 'Amazing Grace', which is often told in ways that downplay his years as a slave-ship captain.

records.name: Hugh Crow
records.scaleNote: Made 13 slaving voyages 1782–1807, seven as master, mostly to Bonny; commanded the Kitty's Amelia, the last legal British slaver (per his 1830 Memoirs and SlaveVoyages).
records.origins: Born in Ramsey, Isle of Man, Crow went to sea young, lost an eye, and entered Liverpool's African trade in the 1780s.
records.role_summary: He traded mainly at Bonny in the Bight of Biafra, where he dealt with King Opobo (Pepple) and described the town's merchants and customs. In July 1807 he sailed the Kitty's Amelia from Liverpool under clearance granted before the 1 May ban, delivering captives to Jamaica in 1808.

roleDetail.d: The Kitty's Amelia carried several hundred captives from Bonny to Jamaica after the Act passed.
His posthumous Memoirs (1830) argue the trade was humane — a self-serving account.

records.legacy: Crow retired in 1808 and died in Liverpool in 1829. His Memoirs remain a much-used, if partisan, source on Bonny and on the end of the legal British trade.

legacyDetail.d: The Bodleian Library reissued his Memoirs for the bicentenary of abolition.

Wikipedia — Hugh Crow

connections.label: last legal voyage under the Act

lineage.name: Edmund and Judith Crow
lineage.note: A tradesman of Ramsey, Isle of Man, and his wife, from whose home Crow went to sea.

lineage.name: Aspinall & Co. (Aspinall family)
lineage.note: The Liverpool slaving house that built the Will in 1797 and employed Crow as her master, notably when he drove off a French privateer in 1800; the family were also partners in the Zong syndicate.

lineage.name: Pepple kings of Bonny
lineage.note: The rulers of Bonny with whom Crow traded for captives over many voyages, and whose town and customs he described at length in his Memoirs.

lineage.name: Thomas Clarke
lineage.note: Liverpool merchant listed in Lloyd's Register (1804) as owner of the Kitty's Amelia; whether he still owned her when Crow took her out in July 1807 for the last legal British slaving voyage is not confirmed.

lineage.name: His executors
lineage.note: At Crow's request his executors compiled his Memoirs, chiefly from his own manuscripts, and published them in London in 1830 with his portrait.

records.today: No publicly documented descendants have been traced. Crow settled in Liverpool in 1817 and died there in 1829; his Memoirs, reissued in 2007 with an introduction by John Pinfold, remain a heavily used (and partisan) source on Bonny. His portrait is held in the Manx National Heritage collections.

records.name: Thomas Phillips
records.scaleNote: Commanded one slaving voyage (Hannibal, 1693–95) on which c. 328 of c. 700 captives died (per his journal and SlaveVoyages); his journal is a standard primary source.
records.origins: A Welsh mariner from Brecon, Phillips commanded the London ship Hannibal, chartered under contract with the Royal African Company.
records.role_summary: He bought c. 700 captives at Ouidah (then capital of the Hueda kingdom) and at Cape Coast and shipped them via São Tomé to Barbados; c. 320–330 died, chiefly of dysentery and smallpox, and some 36 of his crew died too. His journal describes branding, chaining and his 'loss' with frank commercial regret.

roleDetail.d: Mortality of almost half was extreme even for the period.
Phillips complained the RAC paid no freight for the dead — showing how deaths were costed.

records.legacy: His journal was published in Churchill's 'Collection of Voyages' (1732) and is reproduced in many textbooks. Brecon historians have recently researched his crew.

legacyDetail.d: Excerpts are a staple of world-history readers on the Middle Passage.

sources.label: Brecon & Radnor History — Voyage of Despair (the Hannibal)
Wikipedia — Hannibal (slave ship)
Brecon & Radnor Express — Controversial plaque commemorating Brecon's links to slave trader is removed ahead of review
Wikipedia — Jeffrey Jeffreys

lineage.name: William Phillips
lineage.note: Phillips's father in Brecon, from whom he inherited his town house, Harvard House.

lineage.name: Sir Jeffrey Jeffreys
lineage.note: London merchant and MP for Brecon who, with others, owned the Hannibal and engaged his fellow Breconian Phillips to command her on the 1693–94 voyage chartered to the Royal African Company.

lineage.name: Royal African Company
lineage.note: The chartered monopoly that hired the Hannibal and paid her owners (Phillips among them, as a part-owner) freight only for each captive landed alive at Barbados.

lineage.name: Walthoe (publisher) and Churchill's Collection
lineage.note: Phillips's journal was printed in 1732 as 'A Journal of a Voyage Made in the Hannibal of London', which carried his account into the textbooks.

records.today: No publicly documented descendants have been traced; Phillips retired to Brecon after the voyage and died in late 1712 or early 1713, being buried at what is now Brecon Cathedral. In 2010 Brecon Town Council unveiled a plaque honouring him that made no mention of the slave trade; it was taken down in June 2020 before the council's review was complete and is now in storage at Y Gaer, Brecon Museum. Rosemary Caldicott's book 'Voyage of Despair' (2024) reconstructs the voyage and its crew.

records.name: Luke Collingwood
records.scaleNote: Commanded only one voyage, the Zong (1781), on which more than 130 captives were thrown overboard on his orders.
records.origins: Previously the surgeon on Gregson's ship William, Collingwood had no experience as a captain when the Gregson syndicate gave him command of the captured Dutch ship Zorg (renamed Zong) off Cape Coast in 1781.
records.role_summary: Overloaded with c. 440 captives, the Zong lost its way, missed Jamaica and ran short of water; from 29 November 1781 Collingwood and his crew threw more than 130 sick and healthy Africans into the sea so the loss could be claimed on insurance. One man climbed back aboard.

roleDetail.d: Under 'general average', jettisoned cargo could be claimed — deaths from illness could not.

records.legacy: Collingwood died soon after reaching Jamaica, before the court cases. No one was prosecuted for the killings.

legacyDetail.d: Granville Sharp tried to bring murder charges but the authorities refused.

Lancaster City Council — Biographies of individuals involved in the Zong

lineage.name: The William and her master
lineage.note: Collingwood was surgeon on the Gregson syndicate's William; at Cape Coast in March 1781 the William's master bought the captured Dutch ship Zorg for the syndicate and Collingwood got his first command in her.

lineage.name: Gregson syndicate
lineage.note: William, John and James Gregson, with Edward Wilson, George Case and James Aspinall, owned the Zong and later sued her underwriters for the people thrown overboard.

lineage.name: James Aspinall
lineage.note: One of the six Liverpool partners in the Zong; the Aspinall house also owned other slavers, including the Will commanded by Hugh Crow.

lineage.name: James Kelsall
lineage.note: Kelsall, who had also served on the William, was the Zong's mate; suspended after a quarrel, he later said he first opposed the killings, and his affidavit was used by the insurers.

lineage.name: Robert Stubbs
lineage.note: A former slave-ship captain aboard as a passenger, who took charge of the ship when Collingwood fell ill.

lineage.name: Gregson v Gilbert
lineage.note: After Collingwood's death three days after reaching Jamaica, the owners' insurance claim went to court; Lord Mansfield ordered a new trial, which is not recorded as having happened.

lineage.name: Olaudah Equiano and Granville Sharp
lineage.note: Equiano brought the case to Sharp, who tried and failed to have the crew prosecuted for murder, making the Zong a rallying point for abolition.

records.today: No publicly documented descendants of Collingwood have been traced, and no one was ever prosecuted for the killings. The Zong is remembered through J. M. W. Turner's 'The Slave Ship' (1840), a memorial stone at Black River, Jamaica (2007), M. NourbeSe Philip's 'Zong!' (2008) and the film 'Belle' (2013); the owners' profits stayed in the Gregson and allied Liverpool houses.

records.name: Gregson syndicate (William, John & James Gregson)
records.scaleNote: William Gregson had interests in c. 150 slave voyages over 50 years (per Richardson); his ships carried c. 58,000 Africans, of whom c. 9,100 died (per Dalton 2021).
records.origins: William Gregson began as a rope-maker and became one of Liverpool's leading slave merchants, serving as mayor in 1762; his son John was mayor in 1784.
records.role_summary: The syndicate of William, John and James Gregson, son-in-law George Case, Edward Wilson and James Aspinall owned the Zong. After the massacre they claimed c. £30 a head from their underwriters; a jury found for them in 1783, but Lord Mansfield ordered a new trial in Gregson v Gilbert after evidence that the water shortage was the crew's fault.

roleDetail.d: Their insurance suit turned c. 132 murders into a commercial dispute over 'cargo'.
Gregson moved into banking and insurance late in his career.

records.legacy: The Zong did not end the Gregsons' business. Gregson Street in Everton, Liverpool, still bears the family name; the case is now a central symbol in British memory of slavery.

legacyDetail.d: Gregson Street, Everton, is named after William Gregson.

sources.label: Lancaster City Council — Biographies of individuals involved in the Zong

records.name: Alexander Falconbridge
records.scaleNote: Surgeon on four Bristol slaving voyages 1782–87; his 'Account of the Slave Trade on the Coast of Africa' (1788) and parliamentary evidence were key abolitionist testimony.
records.origins: A young surgeon, Falconbridge signed on to Bristol slave ships to earn a living, sailing mainly to Bonny and New Calabar.
records.role_summary: He described the packing of captives below decks, the dancing forced on them, the use of speculums to force-feed those who refused food, and the disease he treated. Recruited by Thomas Clarkson, he accompanied him to collect evidence and testified before Parliament in 1790.

roleDetail.d: His account of the hold so foul he nearly fainted was widely reprinted.
He was sent by the St George's Bay Company to Sierra Leone in 1791 and died at Freetown in 1792.

records.legacy: His wife Anna Maria Falconbridge published a critical 'Narrative of Two Voyages to the River Sierra Leone' (1794). His Account is now freely available and widely used in schools.

legacyDetail.d: Excerpts are a standard Middle Passage document.

sources.label: Project Gutenberg — An Account of the Slave Trade on the Coast of Africa (1788)
Wikipedia — Alexander Falconbridge
Wikipedia — Anna Maria Falconbridge

connections.label: evidence used by the same campaign

lineage.name: Bristol slaving voyages (Tartar, Emilia, Alexander)
lineage.note: He served as surgeon on four slaving voyages, which provided the evidence for his 1788 'Account'.

lineage.name: Thomas Clarkson
lineage.note: The abolitionist recruited Falconbridge in Bristol, used him as guide and armed bodyguard while gathering evidence, and brought him into the abolition committee's work.

lineage.name: Anna Maria Falconbridge (née Horwood)
lineage.note: A Bristol woman who married him in 1788 against her family's wishes, went with him to Sierra Leone in 1791, and wrote the 'Narrative of Two Voyages to the River Sierra Leone' (1794), the first published narrative of Africa by an English woman.

lineage.name: William Falconbridge
lineage.note: His brother travelled with him on the 1791 mission to re-found Granville Town in Sierra Leone.

lineage.name: St George's Bay Company / Sierra Leone Company
lineage.note: The abolitionist-backed company sent him to reorganise the failed Granville Town settlement and employed him as commercial agent at Freetown, dismissing him (with his brother-in-law Charles Horwood) shortly before his death in December 1792.

lineage.name: Isaac DuBois
lineage.note: A Sierra Leone Company employee whom Anna Maria married weeks after Falconbridge's death; the company refused her claim for money owed to her late husband.

records.today: No publicly documented descendants of Alexander Falconbridge have been traced; he died in Freetown in 1792 with no recorded children. His 'Account of the Slave Trade on the Coast of Africa' and Anna Maria's 'Narrative' are both freely available and widely used in teaching.

records.name: James Field Stanfield
records.scaleNote: Common sailor on one Liverpool voyage to Benin (1774–76); 'Observations on a Guinea Voyage' (1788) is the first published account by an ordinary seaman.
records.origins: Born in Ireland and educated in France for the priesthood, Stanfield went to sea instead and signed on to a Liverpool ship bound for Benin in 1774.
records.role_summary: He spent months at a trading post in the Kingdom of Benin while captives were assembled and then sailed to Jamaica, witnessing the deaths of captives and crew alike; he was one of only a few crew survivors. His letters to Clarkson, published by the abolition society in 1788, and his poem 'The Guinea Voyage' (1789) exposed the brutality toward sailors as well as Africans.

roleDetail.d: He stressed the beating, starvation and death of seamen, supporting Clarkson's argument that the trade was a 'grave' for sailors.

records.legacy: He became an actor and theatre manager in northern England; his son, the marine painter Clarkson Stanfield, was named after Thomas Clarkson.

legacyDetail.d: Clarkson Stanfield RA (1793–1867) carried the abolitionist's name.

sources.label: Encyclopedia Virginia — Letter the Third, from Observations on a Guinea Voyage (1788)
Irish Times — The Irishman determined to expose the slave trade (2024)
Wikipedia — James Field Stanfield

lineage.name: Liverpool slaving voyage to Benin
lineage.note: He signed on in Liverpool in September 1774 as a seaman on a ship bound for Benin, which delivered more than 200 Africans to Jamaica.

lineage.name: Thomas Clarkson
lineage.note: The abolitionist to whom Stanfield addressed his 'Observations on a Guinea Voyage' (1788); Stanfield later named his son after him.

lineage.name: Mary Hoad
lineage.note: An artist and actress of Cheltenham whom he married in 1785 while working in the theatre; she was the mother of the painter Clarkson Stanfield.

lineage.name: Clarkson Frederick Stanfield
lineage.note: Born in Sunderland and named after Thomas Clarkson, he became a leading marine painter, a Royal Academician (1835) and a close friend and collaborator of Charles Dickens.

lineage.name: George Clarkson Stanfield
lineage.note: Son of Clarkson Stanfield and a marine and landscape painter trained by his father.

lineage.name: Francis Stanfield
lineage.note: Son of Clarkson Stanfield who became a Catholic priest and hymn composer.

records.today: No living descendants are publicly documented. The family name survives mainly through Clarkson Stanfield's paintings, held in the Royal Collection, Sunderland Museum and Winter Gardens and elsewhere, which carry the abolitionist's name chosen by a former slave-ship sailor.

records.name: William Foster
records.scaleNote: Built and captained the Clotilda, the last known slave ship to reach the US (1860, 110 captives); fined $1,000, the only penalty imposed on anyone involved.
records.origins: Born in Nova Scotia, Foster became a Mobile shipbuilder and in 1855 built the two-masted schooner Clotilda for the Gulf trade.
records.role_summary: Hired by Timothy Meaher, he sailed to Ouidah in 1860 and bought 110 captives from Dahomey's trade, leaving 15 behind when he sighted steamers. He landed them up the Mobile River in July 1860, then burned and scuttled the ship to destroy evidence, keeping some captives himself.

roleDetail.d: Foster's own account of the voyage survives and was used in the wreck identification.
He was fined $1,000 for failing to pay duties/conspiracy; the slave-trading charges were dropped.

records.legacy: He died in Mobile in 1901. The wreck he scuttled was identified in 2019 and is now protected; its discovery revived Clotilda descendant activism.

legacyDetail.d: Alabama Historical Commission identified the Clotilda in May 2019.

sources.label: Encyclopedia of Alabama — Clotilda
National Geographic — Clotilda, America's last slave ship
Wikipedia — Timothy Meaher
Wikipedia — Clotilda (slave ship)

lineage.name: Timothy Meaher
lineage.note: The Mobile shipyard and steamboat owner who backed the 1860 voyage on a wager, hired Foster (a shipbuilder friend) to build or fit out and command the Clotilda, and kept about 30 of the captives himself.

lineage.name: Meaher brothers
lineage.note: Timothy's brothers, who had come with him from Maine to Mobile and held plantations, sawmills and steamboats, took shares of the captives after the landing.

lineage.name: Abile (Celia Lewis) and fifteen others
lineage.note: Foster took 16 of the captives as his share, among them Abile, who after emancipation married Kossola (Cudjo Lewis) in Africatown.

lineage.name: Africatown
lineage.note: The settlement founded by the Clotilda survivors on land they bought near Mobile, whose descendants still live there.

lineage.name: Meaher family
lineage.note: Meaher's heirs leased Africatown-area land to a paper mill in 1926 and long refused comment, before family members issued a public statement in October 2022 acknowledging that his actions had harmed generations.

records.today: No publicly documented descendants of Foster have been traced. The wreck he burned and scuttled was identified in 2019; descendants of the captives, organised in the Clotilda Descendants Association (whose public figures include Joycelyn Davis), lead Africatown's preservation work, and the Africatown Heritage House museum opened in 2023. In October 2022 the Meaher family issued a statement saying it had 'been silent for too long', and in 2023 Meg and Helen Meaher, the only family members who have spoken publicly, met Clotilda descendants on CBS '60 Minutes'.

records.name: Ramón Ferrer
records.scaleNote: Captain and owner of the coastal schooner Amistad; killed in the 1839 revolt. Known from the Amistad court records.
records.origins: A Spanish mariner in Cuba, Ferrer owned and commanded La Amistad, a schooner used in the Cuban coastal trade.
records.role_summary: In late June 1839 he took on 53 Africans newly landed illegally from the Tecora, plus Ruiz and Montes, for a voyage from Havana to Puerto Príncipe. In the revolt led by Sengbe Pieh he and the cook Celestino were killed; his enslaved cabin boy Antonio survived and testified.

roleDetail.d: Coastal schooners like the Amistad distributed newly imported Africans under false 'ladino' papers.

records.legacy: His heirs' claims, and Spain's demand for the ship and 'cargo', fed a diplomatic dispute that lasted into the 1850s.

legacyDetail.d: Spain pressed the US for compensation for years after 1841.

sources.label: US National Archives — Teaching With Documents: The Amistad Case
Wikipedia — La Amistad
Wikipedia — United States v. The Amistad

lineage.name: José Ruiz and Pedro Montes
lineage.note: Spanish merchants who bought 53 newly imported Africans in Havana (49 for Ruiz, 4 for Montes) under false papers and shipped them on Ferrer's schooner; spared in the revolt, they later sued for their 'property' and lost.

lineage.name: Antonio
lineage.note: Ferrer's personal slave, spared to interpret during the revolt; the district court awarded him to Ferrer's heirs, but he is reported to have escaped to New York or Canada with abolitionist help.

lineage.name: Celestino
lineage.note: The enslaved (or free mulatto) cook killed alongside Ferrer in the revolt led by Sengbe Pieh.

lineage.name: Ferrer's heirs
lineage.note: His heirs claimed the ship and Antonio; their and Spain's demands for compensation remained a diplomatic issue between Spain and the US for years.

lineage.name: La Amistad / Ion
lineage.note: The US government auctioned the schooner in 1840 to George Hawford of Newport, Rhode Island, who renamed her Ion.

records.today: No publicly documented descendants of Ferrer have been traced. The Supreme Court freed the Africans in 1841 and 35 returned to Sierra Leone in 1842; the replica Freedom Schooner Amistad (built at Mystic Seaport, 1998–2000) now tells their story.

records.name: The Zong (1781) and Gregson v Gilbert (1783)
records.description: Liverpool-owned slave ship whose crew threw more than 130 Africans overboard from 29 November 1781 so the owners could claim insurance. The owners won a jury verdict in 1783; on the insurers' appeal (Gregson v Gilbert) Lord Mansfield ordered a new trial. Equiano and Granville Sharp publicised the case, which became a turning point for British abolitionism.

records.name: The Brookes (Brooks) and the 1788 diagram
records.description: Liverpool slave ship owned by Joseph Brooks Jr. In late 1788 the Plymouth abolition society (William Elford) published a plan showing captives packed in its decks; the London committee reissued it in 1789 and thousands of copies circulated in Britain, France and the US. It is a schematic projection based on official measurements, not a record of one voyage.

records.name: La Amistad (1839)
records.description: Cuban coastal schooner on which 53 Mende and other West Africans, illegally imported via the Tecora, rose up in July 1839. Seized off Long Island by the USS Washington, the Africans were held in Connecticut; in March 1841 the US Supreme Court (United States v. The Amistad) ruled them free, and survivors returned to Sierra Leone in 1842.

records.name: Henrietta Marie (wreck, 1700)
records.description: London slave ship that sold 191 captives from New Calabar in Jamaica in 1700 (per the Mel Fisher Maritime Museum) and sank on the return leg near the Marquesas Keys, Florida. Found by Mel Fisher's salvors in 1972 and excavated 1983–85, it yielded shackles (some child-sized), trade beads and its bell; it is the largest archaeological collection from an early slave ship. The National Association of Black Scuba Divers placed an underwater memorial there in the early 1990s.

records.name: São José Paquete de África (wreck, 1794)
records.description: Portuguese slave ship that left Lisbon in April 1794, loaded c. 400–500 captives at Mozambique Island for Brazil, and wrecked off Cape Town on 27 December 1794; c. 212 Africans died and survivors were sold at the Cape. Its identification by the Slave Wrecks Project (Smithsonian NMAAHC, Iziko Museums and partners), confirmed in 2014 and announced in June 2015, marked the first time archaeological evidence was recovered from a slave ship known to have sunk with captives aboard; soil from Mozambique Island was scattered over the site.

records.name: The Hannibal (1693–1695)
records.description: London ship commanded by Thomas Phillips under contract with the Royal African Company. It bought c. 700 captives at Ouidah and Cape Coast; c. 328 died before reaching Barbados, mainly of dysentery and smallpox, along with many of the crew. Phillips's journal (1732) is a classic Middle Passage source.

records.name: Creole revolt (1841)
records.description: In November 1841 Madison Washington and 18 others seized the brig Creole, carrying c. 135 enslaved people in the domestic trade from Richmond to New Orleans, and sailed to Nassau in the British Bahamas. British officials freed almost all of them under the 1833 Abolition Act, sparking an Anglo-American dispute; it is often called the most successful slave revolt in US history.

records.name: SlaveVoyages (Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade Database)
records.description: Collaborative database begun by David Eltis and David Richardson (CD-ROM 1999, online 2008, now based at Rice and Emory and partners) documenting c. 36,000 transatlantic and c. 10,000 intra-American slaving voyages. Its estimates put the trade at c. 12.5 million people embarked and c. 10.7 million landed, 1501–1866.

records.name: African Origins (African Names Database)
records.description: Part of SlaveVoyages, it records names, ages, sex and ships of c. 91,000 Africans freed from captured slave ships by the Mixed Commission courts at Havana and Freetown (1808–1862), from Sierra Leone and UK National Archives registers. It invites speakers of African languages to help identify the likely origins of each name.

records.name: Sailors of the slave trade (crimps, debt and death)
records.description: Slave-ship crews were often recruited through crimps and tavern debt in ports such as Bristol's Marsh Street, and some through impressment. Thomas Clarkson, gathering evidence in Bristol and Liverpool in 1787 (using the Seven Stars pub and port muster rolls), showed that sailor death rates on slaving voyages far exceeded other trades; his tables were printed in the 1789 Privy Council report and became a key abolitionist argument.

records.name: Sons of Africa
records.description: London group of Black abolitionists active in the late 1780s–1790s, including Olaudah Equiano and Ottobah Cugoano, who wrote public letters to newspapers, MPs and campaigners such as Granville Sharp in support of abolition.

events.title: Hannibal reaches Barbados
events.text: Thomas Phillips's ship lands c. 372 survivors of c. 700 captives bought at Ouidah; c. 328 died on the crossing.

events.text: Bought out of slavery in Maryland through the Royal African Company, Ayuba sits for William Hoare in London before returning to Gambia in 1734.

events.text: Matilda McCrear dies in Selma, Alabama, the last known person carried in the transatlantic trade.
